summary: Describes extending the IETF Datatracker to record and show how Internet-Drafts progress when they are intended for RFC publication by the IAB, IRTF, or Independent Submissions streams. States and annotations apply once a stream marks a draft as a potential RFC.

plainLanguage.summary: A tracking website follows each document from draft to published RFC. This explains the new steps and notes it needs for documents from three streams outside the main IETF process.

subtitle: Tracking drafts from the IAB, IRTF, and independent authors through to publication as RFCs.

tldr.problem: The IETF Datatracker only tracked documents from the main IETF working group stream, leaving documents from the IAB, IRTF research groups, and independent authors with less visibility about their progress toward publication.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines state machines and annotations for each of the three non-IETF streams, allowing the Datatracker to record which state each draft has reached in its specific stream's process.
tldr.outcome: The Datatracker can now display a document's current status, stream, intended RFC category, and other metadata for IAB, IRTF, and independent submissions, giving visibility into their progress.

today: RFC 6322 is Informational. The Datatracker was enhanced with these states and annotations, allowing the community to monitor the progress of IAB, IRTF, and independent submission documents as they move toward publication.

sections.title: Four Streams of RFC Documents
sections.content:
The IETF is one of four organizations that publish RFCs. The other three are the Internet Architecture Board (IAB), which publishes architectural and policy guidance; the Internet Research Task Force (IRTF), which publishes the output of research groups; and the Independent Submissions Editor (ISE), who publishes documents that do not fit the other streams.

Until this document, the IETF Datatracker—the tool used to track draft-to-RFC progression—only recorded states for documents in the IETF stream. Community members wanted to see the progress of IAB, IRTF, and independent submissions as they moved toward publication.
sections.plainLanguage: Four different groups can publish RFCs. The tracking tool only watched the main IETF group. Now it needs to watch the other three.

sections.title: States and Annotations for Each Stream
sections.content:
Each stream has its own workflow. The IAB stream has states like Candidate IAB Document, Active IAB Document, Parked IAB Document, and Sent to the RFC Editor. Each state can have annotations explaining delays, such as "Waiting for Partner Feedback" or "Revised I-D Needed".

The IRTF stream progresses through research group discussion, group consensus, then moves through the Internet Research Steering Group (IRSG) for review before sending to the RFC Editor. It has states for each of these stages and annotations like "Waiting for Dependency on Other Document" or "IESG Review Completed".

The Independent Submission stream moves from submission through finding reviewers, ISE review, possible IESG review, and eventually to the RFC Editor. Its states and annotations track where the document stands in that process.
sections.plainLanguage: Each stream has its own list of steps and reasons for delays. The tool now knows and displays them.

sections.title: Who Controls the States
sections.content:
For security and accuracy, each stream's managers can modify the states and annotations of documents in their stream. The IAB Chair controls IAB document states. IRTF Research Group Chairs and the IRTF Chair control IRTF document states. The Independent Submissions Editor controls independent submission states.

Each stream owner can grant write access to others in their stream—for example, an RG Chair can delegate state management to a document shepherd. The Datatracker logs all changes and allows comments to be attached to annotations, providing an audit trail and communication record.
sections.plainLanguage: Each stream's leader can update its documents' status in the tracker. Helpers can do it too if given permission.

sections.title: Visibility in the Datatracker
sections.content:
When users look up a draft in the Datatracker, the system displays the document's current stream, approval status, intended RFC category (Informational, Experimental, etc.), last update date, and the assigned document shepherd if one exists. For IRTF documents, it also shows the relevant research group.

When an Internet-Draft moves between streams (for example, from an IRTF research group to the independent submission stream), the Datatracker preserves all previous state history and annotations. When a draft moves out of a stream entirely (because it was not adopted), the Datatracker records that transition.
sections.plainLanguage: When you look up a draft, you see which stream it is in, what step it is on, and who is helping it along.

sections.title: Impact and Scope
sections.content:
The RFC notes that changing tracker states does not affect the security of the Internet. The three streams (IAB, IRTF, ISE) reviewed and approved the document's requirements for their respective workflows, confirming it met their needs.

This document was written in coordination with the IETF Administrative Oversight Committee (IAOC) to formalize the requirements before tool development began. It represents requirements for initial implementation and was not intended to stand as a permanent specification as the tool evolved and features were added.
sections.plainLanguage: Showing status does not break anything. The groups that use it agree this is what they need.
